title: Why pip does nothing inside Blender

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture this. You write a Blender add-on, you type pip install, it works fine, and then Blender says it has never heard of the module. Annoying, right?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Honestly yes. I'd assume pip was broken. What's actually going on?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Blender ships its own Python. So the pip on your system installs packages for a completely different interpreter. Add-ons that need NumPy, meshio or requests all hit that same wall.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the package is installed, just in the wrong house.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. Antoine wrote a small installer for this, for Blender 4.2 and up on Windows. It calls pip through Blender's own interpreter, so the package lands where Blender will actually look.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And where does it put the files? I don't love add-ons that need admin rights.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No admin needed. It uses a per-user scripts modules folder that's writable, and it survives add-on reloads. It also skips packages that already import, so a second run is quick.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What about the interface freezing while pip downloads things?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the other half of the trick. The install runs in a background thread, so Blender stays responsive. But only the main thread may touch the interface, so the popups go through Blender's timers and show up when it's done.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Smart. How do people run it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Two ways. Paste it into the Scripting workspace and hit Run Script, or call it from your add-on's register function so dependencies ship with the add-on.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A few. Restart Blender after the first install, pin your versions because Blender's Python isn't your system's 3.12, and on locked-down corporate PCs pip may be blocked, so you'd bundle wheels by hand.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So users stop asking which Python to use.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the takeaway. You own the dependency list, and users just click. The full write-up has the script and the troubleshooting table.
